intro: Five long reads: why Chinese open-weight models blunt America's AI leverage, what mathematics is for once machines can clear its list of famous problems, a map suggesting the gas between the stars is far from calm, how Rome's sexual freedom belonged only to free men, and a case for Christians taking the paranormal seriously.

stories.headline: Washington cannot sanction a free download
stories.dek: Chinese open-weight models are turning much of AI into a commodity, Max Bessler argues, and commodities make poor chokepoints; America's leverage now lies in chips and clouds.
body: Since the second world war America has treated the global reach of its technology firms as an instrument of state. Export controls on chips, intelligence access to digital platforms, the world's dependence on firms such as Nvidia and Meta: each gives Washington a lever. The playbook assumes America will own the dominant version of whatever technology matters most.

Max Bessler, an Oxford MPhil candidate in international relations and a visiting fellow at the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, argues in Palladium that artificial intelligence may break the pattern. His claim is not that China will overtake America at the frontier. It is that it does not need to. By giving away the weights of capable models, Chinese labs are splitting the AI market into a vast cheap layer and a narrow premium one, and the cheap layer is exactly where coercive power lives.

The two countries' firms have taken opposite routes. OpenAI and Anthropic keep their best models closed, withholding weights and training methods and charging for access. Moonshot, Alibaba, Zhipu and DeepSeek publish the weights of many of theirs, so anyone can run them on their own hardware, and make money instead from consumer apps, cloud hosting, consulting and licensing.
## Generics and brands

Bessler's model of where demand is heading comes from pharmaceuticals. In that industry generic drugs account for about 90% of prescriptions but only 12% of spending; branded drugs take the other 10% of prescriptions and 88% of the money. Buyers pay the premium only when the gap in capability justifies it. He expects AI to settle into the same shape. Routine work such as simple advice, web research and drafting is still often sent to expensive models, but he thinks it will become a baseline feature of cheap ones, leaving the premium tier to complex and as yet unknown applications.

He concedes that Chinese open models trail the American frontier, citing benchmarks from Epoch and METR. His point is that they only have to be good enough for cost-conscious buyers, who can route routine jobs to an open model and pay for Claude when a task demands it.

Vercel reported in September that open-weight models handled 56% of the tokens passing through its gateway in August but only 14% of spending. CNBC reported in July that the share of tokens used by American companies on Chinese models via OpenRouter had stayed above 30% since February, peaking at 46%. Hugging Face found that most of 2025's trending models were Chinese or derived from Chinese ones. Bessler admits the data are murky: Neil Woodford has observed that OpenAI's API alone handles roughly six and a half times as many tokens a month as every model on OpenRouter combined, and firms rarely disclose which models they use.
## How chokepoints work

Each American technology wave, from desktops in the 1970s to cloud in the 2010s, carried Washington's interests abroad. Two cases show the leverage at work. When Washington cut Huawei off from Google's Android in 2019 and from TSMC's chips in 2020, its global smartphone share fell from 20% to almost nothing outside mainland China by 2024. Cisco, which in fiscal 1998 sold $8.5bn of equipment that cost $2.9bn to make, carried much of the world's internet traffic; Glenn Greenwald's No Place to Hide published photographs of NSA staff fitting "beacons" to its routers.

He frames this with Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman's idea of "weaponised interdependence" and Edward Fishman's three tests for a chokepoint: a concentrated, dominant market share; no short-term substitutes; and the ability to inflict asymmetric pain. Fishman had speculated that AI models might qualify. Bessler thinks open weights fail all three. Substitutes are free and improving, so sanctions would hurt little and might provoke targets into building their own. Blacklisting companies that use Chinese models would mostly disrupt American firms and push allies towards sovereign alternatives.

Nor are American incentives aligned. Profit motives discourage American labs from open weights, while Bessler describes Chinese labs as more public-spirited. Nvidia, meanwhile, profits from the data centres that run Chinese models; in July it led more than 270 technology companies in an open letter opposing restrictions on them. OpenAI and Google signed late; Anthropic, which has accused Chinese labs of distilling its Claude models, had not signed.

Here he parts company with Daniel Francis, whose August Palladium essay called the flood of Chinese open models an economic attack on American military development. Francis proposed federal subsidies so that labs reserve their most advanced models for government, release "heavily neutered" public versions and keep weights closed. Bessler accepts that the military stakes are real, and adds a commercial one: a growing commodity layer starves frontier labs of the profits that fund their next models. But he rejects Francis's remedy with a single line: a model that never diffuses is no chokepoint.
## The lesson of memory chips

His historical analogy is Japan's conquest of DRAM. IBM invented the memory chip, but standardisation turned it into a commodity, and NEC, Toshiba and Hitachi pushed Japan's global share to 80% by 1987. After lobbying by Fairchild, National Semiconductor and Intel, Washington turned protectionist: the Semiconductor Industry Association helped create SEMATECH, a joint research consortium, and a bilateral agreement set a goal of "slightly above 20 percent" foreign share of Japan's DRAM market within five years. By the mid-1990s American firms had regained about half the world semiconductor market.

The victory was partial. Korea later took DRAM from Japan, and Silicon Valley survived by moving into higher-value products, while personal computers, microprocessors, workstations and networking all benefited from cheap memory. Japan, in Bessler's phrase, won the battle without winning the longer war. Crucially, DRAM never worked as a coercive chokepoint. There were too many manufacturers and too many substitutes.
## Where the leverage remains

Bessler's prescription is to stop trying to control the model layer and concentrate on the two layers that still have chokepoint properties. The first is compute. He cites figures putting American AI compute at 39.7m petaflops against 400,000 in China, and Nvidia's share of the AI chip market at more than 85%. Chinese labs still lack cutting-edge chips, he notes, though that has not stopped their open models from spreading, and America's own build-out is constrained more by power and permitting than by chip supply.

The second is cloud hosting and inference, where American providers hold more than 70% of the market. Moonshot is negotiating to offer Kimi K3 on the three largest. Thomson Reuters and Harvey have built products on Qwen and Kimi K3. That, Bessler suggests, is how value may flow if the model layer commoditises: to the American application companies that bill customers directly, as Japan's memory profits once flowed to California, while Moonshot and Alibaba struggle to profit even as their models do the work.

His conclusion is modest in its claims about the future. The AI market will probably divide whatever Washington does, and nobody knows what that will do to the frontier labs' economics. Policy should keep chip controls narrow and keep the cloud American. As he puts it, America may no longer be able to tell you which model to use, but it can own where that model runs.
stories.counterpoint: The generic-drug analogy may flatter the cheap tier: if frontier capability keeps compounding, the premium segment could swallow far more than 10% of valuable work, and the commodity layer could matter less than token counts suggest. Bessler's own measurement caveats cut against his evidence, since OpenRouter and Vercel are a small and unrepresentative slice of total usage. And cloud dominance is itself fragile leverage: the more Washington uses it, the faster allies may build sovereign hosting.
stories.why: Much of the AI policy debate assumes the model is the strategic asset. If Bessler is right, export controls aimed at weights are fighting the last war, and the real contest is over data centres, power and the hosting contracts that decide where inference happens. That reframes questions from chip licensing to which clouds allies trust with their workloads.
questions: If cheap open models become good enough for most routine work, what share of AI's economic value do you expect the premium tier to keep?
Is a technology that cannot be used for coercion less strategically important, or simply important in a different way?
Does the DRAM story suggest that losing the commodity layer is a defeat, or a sensible division of labour?

source.title: The Limits of AI as an Economic Weapon
source.author: Max Bessler

stories.headline: When machines clear the list, mathematicians need new problems
stories.dek: Atoosa Kasirzadeh argues that AI is ending a narrow, trophy-hunting idea of mathematical progress, and that the field should rebuild around problems the world throws at it.
body: The past year has been disorienting for mathematicians. AI systems have completed a formalisation of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem; a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem has been claimed; hundreds of manuscripts each assert a proof of some famous conjecture. On October 26th another Clay Millennium Prize problem was reportedly solved by a machine. The reactions have ranged from exhilaration to something close to mourning.

Atoosa Kasirzadeh, a philosopher and mathematician who is a research scientist at the DeepMind Institute and an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon, catalogues those reactions in Noema. A PhD student, Kirwin Hampshire, wrote in July of "The Dark Night of Mathematics" and a spiritual crisis. An unnamed Fields medallist ended a talk by calling for "new theories of care and love". The philosopher Logan Graves suggested human mathematicians might come to resemble priests, then monks. Terence Tao, by contrast, forecast a community that would "emerge stronger" in an age of "proof post-scarcity"; Daniel Litt of the University of Toronto was broadly optimistic but worried about institutions and training; Steven Strogatz of Cornell declared the age of the lone hero over.

Each, Kasirzadeh thinks, grasps part of the problem. Underneath them lie four questions: what mathematical progress actually is; how AI disrupts mathematicians' epistemic and creative agency; how future mathematicians should be educated; and how incentives, rewards and credit should be reorganised. Her essay concentrates on the first, because she thinks the answer to it shapes the rest.
## The checklist model

The dominant picture she calls the checklist model. Progress means solving well-defined problems set in advance: Olympiad questions, Fermat, Freek Wiedijk's list of 100 theorems to formalise, the Millennium problems. Its appeal is that it is tidy and measurable, and it underwrites mathematics' prestige economy of Olympiad medals, Fields Medals and prizes, as well as AI's benchmark culture, which loves a crisp target.

AI, she argues, is making this model unsustainable. Once machines can tick items off the list, the norm that reserved such achievements for human genius loses its social weight. Grief at that loss is valid, she says, but staying in it prevents adaptation. And the checklist was never a full description of the discipline anyway: G.H. Hardy, who died in 1947, boasted that he had never done anything "useful", a pose that only makes sense if mathematics is a sequence of self-set puzzles.
## The generative encounter

Her alternative is what she calls the generative encounter model, in which mathematics grows out of collisions with practical and social problems that nobody would have thought to put on a list. Her chief example is George Dantzig. In 1939, arriving late to a class at Berkeley, he copied two problems from the blackboard, assumed they were homework and solved them; they were famous open problems, and about six weeks later Jerzy Neyman rushed to his door eager to publish.

The more consequential episode came later. As an adviser to the US Air Force Comptroller, Dantzig was asked to mechanise military logistics, then managed by thousands of clerks working by trial and error. He recast the problem as a linear objective subject to linear constraints, showed that the optimum lies at a vertex of a convex polyhedron, and devised the simplex algorithm to find it. Because aeroplanes and pilots come in whole numbers, a further constraint produced integer programming, and further branches followed. Dantzig also gathered a community of "linear programmers" that drew in operations researchers and economists.

Norbert Wiener supplies a second case. Asked how to aim anti-aircraft guns at evasive pilots, he reframed the pilot as part of a feedback system and treated the problem statistically, yielding filtering and prediction theory and, in his 1948 book Cybernetics, a new field. The Macy Conferences of the late 1940s and early 1950s brought biologists, psychiatrists, anthropologists and engineers together around it. Wiener's predictor was never deployed, because a simpler Bell Labs design won the contract. The mathematics endured anyway. None of these problems, Kasirzadeh notes, would have appeared on anyone's checklist.
## Against the pure-applied snobbery

She recalls a national conference for mathematics graduate students in Canada at which peers in analytic number theory dismissed operations research as "not real mathematics". She sees that hierarchy as a cultural prejudice the checklist model reinforced, and one AI now forces the field to drop. Dantzig himself rejected it, calling himself simply "a mathematician" and his purist colleagues snobs; real-world problems, he said, are all dirty, and every model is an approximation. Relevance energised him rather than constrained him. A messy encounter with the world, Kasirzadeh concludes, can produce pure mathematics.
## What to work on instead

Restructuring credit could cultivate Dantzig-style thinkers who use AI to deepen their creative work. The key question, she suggests, should shift from "Who proved it?" to "Who decided this was worth proving, and how did we ensure it was right?" There are precedents for collective credit: the Polymath projects, the Lean community's Mathlib library, and the effort to formalise Fermat.

She names four clusters of problems she considers urgent. The first is provably safe cyber-infrastructure, given how fragile digital systems are. The second is the epistemic mechanics of deep learning, since understanding of why neural networks generalise remains in its infancy. The third is the mathematics of multi-agent control, drawing on game theory and mechanism design to understand how interacting AI agents can be aligned. The fourth is the epistemology of machine-generated proofs: results too long or alien for humans to check, which call for new techniques of explanation and interactive verification. On that point she is explicit that the field should not rush to rely on proofs people cannot yet check.
## Where mathematics comes from

Kasirzadeh briefly revisits the old philosophical quarrel. George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez locate mathematics in embodied cognition; Platonists say it is discovered; formalists treat it as a rule-governed game whose truths resemble legal chess moves. She declines to adjudicate, but observes that every position places mathematics' origin in some kind of encounter, and that AI has now joined the encounter as a participant.

A revolution in automated proof, she stresses, guarantees nothing about the field's future. Its direction depends on what people build: how results are verified, how credit is assigned, how students are trained and who gets to take part. She acknowledges the deepest fear among some pure mathematicians, that a future superintelligence might automate not just proving but choosing what is worth proving, and so automate human purpose itself. Her answer is that the long dream of formalisation, running from mathematical logic to Lean, carries obligations to attend to its consequences. A true golden age, she concludes, may have just begun, and the transition is where it will be made.
stories.counterpoint: Kasirzadeh may be too quick to dismiss the checklist. Named problems have served as coordination devices that concentrate effort and certify quality, and the generative model offers no comparably clear way to tell progress from fashion. Her four urgent problem clusters also sit conveniently close to AI labs' own priorities, which invites the question of whether 'encounter' simply means mathematics in the service of whoever funds the encounter.
stories.why: The way a discipline defines progress decides whom it trains, whom it rewards and what it ignores. If machines can clear the list, mathematics either finds a new account of its purpose or shrinks into a verification service. The same question is coming for other fields where AI can now hit benchmarks.
questions: If an AI proves a famous conjecture, who, if anyone, deserves the credit, and does the question matter?
Is choosing which problems are worth solving a skill that can be taught, or only one that is learned through practice?
Which human activities in your own field are most like ticking off a checklist, and which are generative encounters?

source.title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress
source.author: Atoosa Kasirzadeh

stories.headline: The space between the stars is restless
stories.dek: A new three-dimensional map suggests that much of the galaxy's interstellar gas sits in a state textbook theory says should barely exist, which may help explain why stars form so slowly.
body: Space is not empty. Between the stars drifts a thin fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms, most of it left over from the Big Bang and topped up by stars that shed gas and dust as they are born and as they die. In 2020 NASA's New Horizons probe, beyond the orbit of Pluto, measured a proxy for its density and found about 130 hydrogen atoms per litre. Sparse as that is, across the volume of a galaxy it is the raw material for every future star.

Because this interstellar medium changes so slowly, Perri Thaler writes in Quanta, astronomers spent roughly half a century treating its details as settled background. A new map, if it survives scrutiny, suggests that background is anything but calm. Much of the gas near the Sun appears to be caught in an unstable, in-between condition that the standard picture says should hardly exist at all.
## A tidy theory from 1969

The textbook account dates to 1969, when George Field, Donald Goldsmith and Harm Habing proposed that interstellar gas settles into two stable phases. In one, gravity pulls gas together into cold clouds at around 100 kelvins, roughly minus 173°C. In the other, gas too hot to collapse is warmed by ultraviolet light from nearby stars and holds steady near 8,000 kelvins. Gas in between was expected to move quickly into one state or the other, so very little should be found lingering at intermediate temperatures.

In 1977 Chris McKee and Jeremiah Ostriker added a third ingredient: very hot plasma, at about half a million kelvins, near the shock fronts of supernovae. But they too assumed that the atomic gas outside those blast zones sat in a calm, pressure-balanced equilibrium. The resulting picture was of a galaxy whose space between stars was layered, stable and essentially predictable.

Testing that picture proved hard. Cold atomic hydrogen emits no visible light. Astronomers detect it through a faint radio signal at a wavelength of 21 centimetres, produced by a rare flip in the spin of hydrogen atoms. But a telescope pointed along a single line of sight picks up the overlapping signals of every cloud in that direction, rather like trying to separate a stack of coloured plastic sheets by looking straight through them. Working out what lies where, and at what temperature, was close to impossible.
## Gaia's gift

The breakthrough came from an instrument built for something else. The European Space Agency's Gaia telescope, launched in 2013 and operated until 2025, observed almost two billion stars and measured their distances by parallax, the small apparent shift in a star's position as the Earth moves round the Sun. Scientists are still working through its data.

Knowing how far away each star is allowed researchers to study how its light dims and reddens as it passes through intervening dust, and so to work out where the dust lies in three dimensions. Gregory Green of Westlake University in Hangzhou explains the difficulty: many different arrangements of the interstellar medium can fit the same observations, and finding the most physically plausible one gets harder as the data grow. In 2024 a team nonetheless produced a continuous 3D dust map covering a sphere more than 4,000 light-years across, centred on the Sun. It showed where dust clumped but not whether that material was hot or cold. A second map, of heating, was needed.
## Unexpected middle ground

That second step came from the Technion in Haifa. Jonathan Shelest, a student there, was drawn into the problem after a 2024 lecture by his professor, Shmuel Bialy, on structures such as the Pillars of Creation; Bialy was looking for a student to work on 3D mapping of the interstellar medium. Shelest started from the 2024 dust map. Bialy, meanwhile, met Troy Porter of Stanford University at a conference and learned that Porter had built an as-yet-unpublished map of the ultraviolet radiation that heats interstellar gas.

The team merged the two data sets, about 200 gigabytes in all, and compared dust density with radiation intensity point by point to estimate where gas should be hot or cold. The result surprised them. Across the Sun's galactic neighbourhood, 27% of the interstellar medium was cold and 32% warm. The remaining 41% sat in the intermediate, unstable range that older theory said should be nearly empty. Shelest assumed at first that he had made a mistake, but found no sign of artefacts or noise. The unstable gas formed large, continuous layers wrapped around the cold clouds.

Adam Ginsburg of the University of Florida reads the result as a sign that something is constantly stirring gas that static theory would leave at rest. His colleague Desika Narayanan offers an analogy with blood carrying oxygen and waste around a body: energy is always being moved, and the medium is always in flux.
## Reasons for caution

The paper was posted on arXiv in July 2026 and is still under peer review. Shelest received a stream of messages from interested astronomers, but researchers quoted by Thaler are wary of rewriting textbooks yet. McKee, one of the authors of the 1977 model, worries that the method may overstate unstable gas if cold and warm regions lie too close together to be told apart. Philipp Frank of the Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology at Stanford points out that the team used an "ensemble-averaged mean", a technique that tends to smooth out sharp transitions. That could make abrupt boundaries between cold and warm gas look gradual and so inflate the unstable fraction.

Shelest and Bialy accept that limited resolution and smoothing are real problems. But they argue that blurring alone cannot explain most of what they found. When they reran the analysis using a lower-resolution dust map, the unstable fraction changed by only about 5%.
## Why stars are slow

If the finding holds, it bears on one of astrophysics' persistent puzzles. Galaxies are strikingly inefficient at turning gas into stars, and simulations have struggled to explain why. A medium that is constantly being heated and cooled, churned rather than settled, might be part of the answer. Anna Rosen of San Diego State University notes that stellar feedback heats and pushes surrounding gas, suppressing further star formation. Existing models, she says, offer useful but static snapshots of hot and cold gas, while much of the action happens in between.

For now the map is a provisional result built on a stack of inferences: distances from parallax, dust from reddening, heating from a separate radiation model, temperature from the combination. Each layer adds uncertainty. But the direction of the evidence is striking. The space between the stars may be less a quiet backdrop than a restless system, and astronomers have only just acquired the tools to watch it move.
stories.counterpoint: The headline 41% is a modelled quantity, not a direct temperature measurement, and it rests on combining two maps built by different methods at limited resolution. Critics such as Philipp Frank have identified a plausible mechanism, statistical smoothing, by which the unstable fraction could be inflated, and a single sensitivity test at lower resolution does not rule out bias at the scales that matter. Until independent methods, such as targeted 21-centimetre observations, confirm the result, the old two-phase picture should be treated as challenged rather than overturned.
stories.why: Star formation sets the pace at which galaxies evolve, build heavy elements and form planets, so a better account of why it is so inefficient would ripple through astrophysics. The episode also shows how a survey designed for one purpose, measuring stellar distances, can reopen questions that had been closed for half a century.
questions: How much confidence should a result earn when it is built from several layers of inference rather than a direct measurement?
Why might a scientific community leave a 'settled' background question unexamined for fifty years?
What other apparently static systems might look turbulent once we can map them in three dimensions?

source.title: A New Map of 'Empty' Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
source.author: Perri Thaler

stories.headline: Rome's sexual freedom belonged to free men
stories.dek: Reviewing Kyle Harper's From Shame to Sin, Samuel Hughes argues that the familiar story of tolerant pagans and repressive Christians gets both halves wrong.
body: There is a story about sex in the ancient world that most educated people absorb without ever examining it. The Greeks and Romans, it runs, were relaxed and affirming about desire in all its forms; then Christianity arrived and smothered that openness under guilt, prohibition and shame. The story is useful to people with very different agendas, which is perhaps why it has survived so long.

Samuel Hughes, an editor at Works in Progress, admits he believed it until he read Kyle Harper's From Shame to Sin: The Christian Transformation of Sexual Morality in Late Antiquity. His review argues that the standard picture is not entirely wrong but is fundamentally misleading, because it leaves out most of what mattered. Roman tolerance was real, but narrow and predatory. The Christian transformation was real too, but stranger and more mixed than either its admirers or its critics tend to allow.
## A licence, not a liberation

In some respects Roman norms were indeed permissive. Free men could have sex with their male and female slaves and with prostitutes, children among them. There was no expectation that a husband be faithful to his wife; extramarital sex was broadly acceptable in principle, even if it hurt her. Most men, Hughes suggests, were probably what we would now call bisexual, with a personal preference for boys or for women rather than a fixed identity. Only a minority of Romans owned slaves, but slave prostitution was widespread, so coerced sex was common and cheap: Hughes puts the price at roughly that of a loaf of bread.

The permissiveness stopped abruptly at the boundaries of status and sex. Women were expected to be virgins at marriage and faithful afterwards, a pattern common to most premodern societies. Classical authors rarely mention sex between women, and when they do it is to mock it. Women lived under strict norms of modesty; in the Greek-speaking provinces many seem to have worn face veils in public.

The rules among men were the most distinctive. The Lex Scantinia, a law now lost and known only from later references, appears to have punished men who penetrated free Roman men or boys, and men who allowed themselves to be penetrated; the latter were called semivir, "half man". Being penetrated was simply incompatible with the dignity of a free Roman male. Slaves, by contrast, were property, described in one memorable phrase as "breathing furniture". What modern readers call Roman tolerance of homosexuality was, on Hughes's reading, a licence for free men to use people of unfree status. The Greek east was somewhat more flexible, allowing freeborn youths to be penetrated during adolescence but not afterwards.
## The novelty of fidelity

Christianity largely overturned this order. Sex within marriage was tolerated, if grudgingly; all sex outside it was condemned, and some forms were banned by law. But the change Hughes thinks hardest to overstate is the idea that men, too, owed fidelity.

Romans allowed a man only one wife but did not expect him to be faithful to her. Judaism condemned adultery but permitted men several wives. Early Christians fused the two, combining the Jewish ban on sex outside marriage with Roman monogamy, and so produced an ideal of mutual fidelity binding on both sexes. Hughes says it is not clear that this ideal was ever arrived at independently by another major civilisation, and he wonders aloud whether it will outlast Christianity's decline in Europe.

The early sources can sound startlingly modern. John Chrysostom insisted that a married man's affairs with prostitutes, slaves or other unmarried women were adultery, not merely sleeping with another man's wife. Pelagius complained that laws made by men were biased against women. Hughes is careful not to overclaim: the early Christians were not consistent feminists. But at times they sounded like them.
## Mercy at the margins

Slavery is where the gap between principle and practice was widest. In theory, Christianity located a person's moral worth in their relationship to God rather than their rank, an idea with obvious abolitionist potential. In practice it rarely led anyone to question slavery, and most early Christians accepted it. Gregory of Nyssa is the first recorded abolitionist. What Christians did do was begin to limit the worst forms of exploitation.

Hughes's clearest example is a sustained imperial campaign against forced prostitution. In 428 the government banned pimps, fathers and slave-owners from selling women into involuntary sex. Offenders were to be sent to the public mines, a penalty the law itself described as lighter than the suffering of a woman forced into sex against her will. The law also protected free women pushed into prostitution by poverty, who could appeal for help to bishops, judges or municipal officials known as defensors. Here, at least, moral concern was being extended to people the classical world had not counted.
## A gloomy view of desire

If Christianity humanised sexual morality in some respects, it was bleak in others. Hughes notes that medieval Christians sometimes saw human desire as having affinities with the love of God, in its longing, self-surrender and sense of incompleteness, and so as potentially noble. Did the early church share that view? Harper's evidence suggests not, beyond very limited exceptions. Early writers were relentlessly negative about desire. The most generous treated it as a morally neutral animal appetite; the common view held it sinful. Virginity was ranked above marriage, which was tolerated chiefly for procreation and as a concession to weakness, though Christians still prized friendship and charity between spouses.
## Seventeen centuries of masks

Hughes's conclusion is that the early Christians were complex. Their restrictiveness sprang partly from suspicion of desire and partly from extending moral concern to people who had no rights in the ancient world, women sold into prostitution among them. Yet that extension was haphazard, and the open, predatory sexuality of antiquity often carried on beneath a Christian surface.

He ends by borrowing a line of George Orwell's about illusions and masks, and applies it to a whole civilisation. Europeans, Hughes suggests, lived under a Christian illusion for almost seventeen centuries, and it changed them. The popular myth about sex in antiquity therefore errs twice. It mistakes a privilege of free men for freedom, and it mistakes a demanding, inconsistent and genuinely novel moral revolution for mere repression.
stories.counterpoint: A short review of a single, if celebrated, book cannot settle a contested historiography; scholars disagree about how widely laws such as the Lex Scantinia were enforced, and evidence from elite authors may not reflect ordinary sexual life. Hughes's portrait of early Christian views of desire as 'relentlessly negative' may also underweight the patristic voices that spoke of rightly ordered love and complicate the picture. And crediting Christianity with mutual fidelity risks treating ideals as practice when, by Hughes's own account, practice often lagged far behind.
stories.why: The tolerant-pagan, repressive-Christian myth shapes current arguments about sexual ethics on all sides. Seeing that Roman 'freedom' rested on slavery and status, and that Christian norms extended protection to the powerless, changes what is actually at stake when people ask whether those norms will survive. For teachers and preachers it offers a more honest history than either triumphalism or apology.
questions: If an ideal such as mutual fidelity arose from a particular religious tradition, can it outlast that tradition's decline?
Why do popular histories so often flatten complex moral changes into simple stories of liberation or repression?
How should we judge a moral revolution that was sincere in principle but haphazard in practice?

stories.headline: Christians should not laugh at ghost stories
stories.dek: Ian Olson argues that believers who confess angels and the resurrection have no business dismissing the paranormal, and proposes an apocalyptic framework for discerning it without fear or fascination.
body: Many Christians hold two attitudes that sit awkwardly together. They confess angels, prophecy, the virgin birth, the resurrection and the real efficacy of the sacraments. Yet when someone reports a ghost, a precognitive dream or an encounter they cannot explain, the same believers often reach for the sceptic's vocabulary of delusion and fraud. Ian Olson, writing in Mere Orthodoxy, thinks this is inconsistent, and pastorally costly.

He concedes that some Christians take such reports seriously. His thesis is that paranormal phenomena lie close enough to religious experience that the church has good reason to examine them and to locate them within a Christian account of reality, rather than leaving that task to secular researchers or to the occult. The essay is less a defence of any particular claim than an argument about what a biblical worldview should leave room for.
## A bounded affinity

Olson starts from the sociology of religion, where scholars speak of a "bounded affinity" between religion and the paranormal: people open to one tend to be open to the other, within limits. He draws especially on Jeffrey Kripal, whose book How to Think Impossibly advances an "experience-source hypothesis": that religious convictions may arise from genuine experiences, not solely from social construction or deception. Kripal links Edmund Husserl's phenomenological method, which brackets questions of ultimate reality to attend to what appears, with medieval apophatic theology's refusal to say too much about God. Olson, for his part, criticises contemporary religious studies for a historicism that flattens its subject by cataloguing beliefs from within an assumed naturalism.
## Why believers scoff

Why, then, do so many Christians dismiss the paranormal? Olson offers three reasons. Some appeal to Colossians 2:15, Christ's triumph over the principalities and powers, as though victory meant the powers were no longer worth noticing; he sees in this a risk of triumphalism. Others hold that the gospel swept away ancient superstition. Olson rejects the universal form of that claim, warning that to call every such report false is itself a kind of false witness, and he connects the idea to the naturalist narrative of disenchantment examined in Peter Harrison's work.

The deepest motive, he suggests, is fear. The strange threatens our illusion of control. He reads Psalm 30:6, "in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved", and 1 Corinthians 10:12, the warning that whoever thinks he stands should take heed lest he fall, as cautions against presumed invulnerability. Confidence in Christ can mask spiritual pride. Acknowledging that strange things happen, he insists, is not the same as preoccupation with them, still less worship.
## Real dangers

Olson does not pretend the subject is safe. He cites the researcher John Keel's warning about "false illumination": entities that manipulate people through their own beliefs and then discredit them. He identifies three conventional Christian responses, denial, fearful acknowledgment and veneration, and rejects all three. Believers, he argues, can acknowledge such realities without servile fear, because hostile powers can harm people only so far as people give them room.
## Encounter without ontology

His constructive proposal is the heart of the essay. Christians should commit to a "phenomenology of encounter" without committing to an ontology of what is encountered. In other words, take seriously what people actually experienced, without rushing to classify it. The governing text is 1 John 4:1, "test the spirits", and Olson models that testing on God's own "Yes" and "No" to fallen humanity. He borrows Karl Barth's notion of "theological exorcism", a form of unbelief grounded in faith, as the posture the church should adopt.

Scripture, he notes, complicates any simple sorting of spiritual beings into categories. In the synagogue at Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28; Luke 4:31–37), an unclean spirit speaks the truth about Jesus' identity without speaking for God. Paul in Galatians 4:8 refers to beings that are "by nature no gods" to which people were once enslaved, suggesting that God may permit and use such powers. Angelic encounters in Scripture habitually begin with "Be not afraid", and Ezekiel's visions show how strange the accompaniments of God's speech can be. Olson therefore urges that eyewitness accounts be judged on what actually happened, not forced at once into the boxes marked "angelic" and "demonic". He draws on Keel and Jacques Vallée, who observed that reports of UFOs resemble older accounts of preternatural beings and that such phenomena seem to adapt to the culture in which they appear.
## Re-enchantment is not the gospel

Olson warns Christians against welcoming every sign of renewed spiritual interest. People weary of a disenchanted world will be drawn to the paranormal, but enchantment is not intrinsically Christian. Uninstructed seekers are vulnerable to false illumination, and plenty of evangelists stand ready to offer them a new gospel.

To describe what such encounters do to people, he adapts Paul Tillich's phrase "ontological shock". He then connects that shock to New Testament apocalyptic, in which the age to come breaks into "the present evil age" (Galatians 1:4). This is the essay's doctrinal centre of gravity. The world can be what it is without being recognised for what it is; hence the need for revelation. Olson points to John 9:39–41 and Romans 1:18–23 on blindness to truth, and to the repeated charge that Jesus' own works came from demons (Matthew 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15; John 7:20 and 10:20). Unusual phenomena do not interpret themselves, and even true signs can be read perversely. He also cautions against presumption in reading Romans 8, and argues that a worldview with no room for the eerie fails, in the end, to love the people who have had such experiences.
## A pastoral calling

Olson's conclusion is practical. Christians should offer pastoral care to people shaken by paranormal experiences, guide them towards Christ, and avoid both dismissal and credulity. He grounds this in John 20:21, where the risen Christ sends the disciples into the world as the Father sent him, and in the church's vocation to bear witness against forces that degrade those made in God's image. He closes with questions rather than answers: what does your theology allow you to see, and does it leave any room for mystery?

Olson's essay is primarily doctrinal and apologetic, with a substantial strand of cultural diagnosis. Its exegesis is often brief and topical rather than sustained, and some of its supporting claims rest on popular or contested sources. But its central move, to separate faithful attention to experience from premature judgments about its nature, gives pastors a usable framework for conversations many now find themselves having.
stories.counterpoint: Bracketing ontology may be harder in pastoral practice than Olson allows: Scripture's instruction to test the spirits presumes a verdict, and a seeker in distress needs to know whether what they met is to be resisted. His reliance on Keel, Vallée and Kripal also imports frameworks whose own assumptions are far from Christian, and the essay gives little attention to how much of what people report may be shaped by expectation, suggestion or illness rather than any external agency.
stories.why: Interest in the paranormal is rising, and many congregations include people with experiences they are embarrassed to mention. Olson offers preachers and teachers a way to take such reports seriously without endorsing them, rooted in 1 John 4:1 and New Testament apocalyptic. It is also a useful test of whether a church's working theology is quietly more naturalist than its creed.
questions: Does your own reaction to reports of the paranormal owe more to Scripture or to modern scepticism?
How can a church test the spirits without either credulity or contempt for the person reporting the experience?
What would it look like to preach Galatians 1:4's 'present evil age' as a present reality rather than a figure of speech?
